source.title: Internalizing Safety Understanding in Large Reasoning Models via Verification
source.authors: Yi Zhang; Yu-Xin Chen; Leheng Sheng; Dong-Cheng Zhang; Chao-Chao Lu; Xiang Wang; An Zhang

page_placements.theme: Explicit and intermediate safety reasoning can improve robustness

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some tables are flattened in the supplied text, so their values cannot always be assigned confidently to individual models and methods.
record.tranche_reason: It measures per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful trajectories, directly testing the token-position concentration claim with a different alignment method and model setting.
record.gate_note: The study also reports many safety-benchmark results for its proposed SInternal training and baseline methods. Those results do not test whether a few harmful or benign fine-tuning examples erode safety, or whether compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes bypass safety. Flattened Table 1 and Table 2 values are not assigned to individual conditions because the supplied layout does not support reliable assignment.
record.test_reason: The study proposes SInternal, verification-based safety training for reasoning models, and reports mainly its own safety, over-refusal and reasoning scores against baselines. Its only link to the claim is Figure 5, which borrows the per-token KL analysis from Qi et al. as a diagnostic. The text says only that SInternal shows higher KL than the other methods 'across different token indices'. It gives no position-wise values. It does not say whether the aligned–base divergence is concentrated in early tokens (V3). It does not test robustness to prefilling or other attacks that get past the opening (V4/V7). Its safety gains are benchmark ASR results for its own method, not a test of whether a deepening fix holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that answer-centric alignment leaves a gap between safe generation and safety verification. They find that training only on verification of the model's own answers (SInternal) improves robustness to unseen and reasoning-specific jailbreaks while preserving reasoning and avoiding over-refusal. They also find it is a better initialization for GRPO. The KL figure is offered only as qualitative 'evidence of deeper alignment': higher KL than baselines across token indices, with no positional analysis.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of fine-tuning on a few harmful or benign examples to test refusal erosion, the study fine-tunes LRMs on approximately 6,000 expert-generated verification trajectories based on the model's own responses, then optionally applies GRPO. It measures per-token KL on harmful trajectories.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across model checkpoints, alignment methods, and attack benchmarks. The paper also reports preserved defense and over-refusal results when changing the safety specification, but does not give numerical per-token KL values by position.

fits_no_version.finding: Verification-classification F1 differs across Base, STAR-1, GRPO and SInternal. SInternal reaches 85.9–89.3 while answer-centric methods do not consistently beat random (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Answer-centric safety training does not instill the ability to verify the safety of candidate answers; verification training does.

fits_no_version.finding: SInternal triggers safety-oriented reasoning in 50.4% of WildJailbreak cases, versus 16.0% for Base and 28.4% for STAR-1. Conditional safety is near-perfect for all three (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verification training increases spontaneous safety reasoning in LRM chains of thought.

fits_no_version.finding: SInternal raises overall safety under WildJailbreak to 78.8%, versus 30.4% for Base and 59.6% for STAR-1, and lowers OOD jailbreak ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training only on self-response safety verification transfers to safer generation under jailbreaks.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Figure 5 is described qualitatively without numerical KL values by token position. The supplied Table 1 and Table 2 layout is flattened, preventing reliable assignment of many scores to model-method combinations. The paper reports point estimates without uncertainty measures.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 2 contain many benchmark scores for Base, SafeChain, STAR-1, SInternal, and their GRPO variants. They were not extracted because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably associate their values with individual models, methods, and metrics. Other SInternal safety, over-refusal, reasoning, ablation, and data-scale results were not included because they do not directly test the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning attack on aligned models.
Whether aligned–base per-token KL concentrates in early positions; Figure 5 is described only comparatively, with no numbers.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. HCoT and roleplay jailbreaks are prompt-level attacks and are not broken down by mechanism.
No localization analysis; LoRA rank 16 is a training setting only.
No test of why alignment is shallow.
No test that SInternal spreads safety beyond the first tokens in a way that resists prefilling or fine-tuning attacks. There are only qualitative KL claims and benchmark ASR.

missing.what: Position-wise per-token KL values (aligned vs base on harmful trajectories) for each method, needed to judge V3/V7.

record.verdict_notes: Downgraded from tests/T1 to uses_without_test/T4. The Qi et al. KL analysis is used as a diagnostic for the study's own method. The text gives no positional numbers and no claim about where the divergence concentrates, so the reader's 'challenges V3' and 'supports V7' labels are not warranted. Tables 1–2 are readable in part, but they report the study's own method benchmarks and bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a few to a few hundred harmful fine-tuning examples increase harmful compliance or remove refusal.
Whether ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data increases harmful compliance.
The text gives no numerical KL values by response position and does not establish that divergence is evenly distributed.
The study evaluates jailbreaks, including reasoning-based attacks, but does not test compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypass interventions.
LoRA rank is stated, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
The study does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
SInternal is not explicitly trained with an objective to spread safety across response positions; the study tests its per-token KL pattern and safety performance under attacks.

relation.reason: The study applies the original per-token KL diagnostic to its trained models and explicitly interprets the resulting differences across token positions as deeper alignment. This is qualitative evidence bearing on V7, although it does not establish the original V3 concentration pattern or test prefill robustness.

tranche.reason: Figure 5 and Section 5.3.2 report the study's own per-token KL analysis in large reasoning models: SInternal and SInternal (GRPO) maintain higher divergence across token indices. Together with jailbreak evaluations, this bears on V7 deepening fixes in a new setting, beyond reporting only method performance.

source_check.notes: Figure 5's qualitative V7 evidence is missing from the listed rows; the extracted text supplies no numerical KL values. Table 4 uses GPT-4o to assess verification and resulting safety; its caption describes attacks with WildJailbreak as the example.

reader_labels.reason: The text describes higher per-token KL across different token indices rather than a difference confined to the opening positions; this challenges first-token concentration, though the figure supplies no numerical position-wise values (r1, r2).
